title: Quoting Ted Sanders
summary:
In general, LLM performance is incredibly multidimensional. There's no guarantee of a fixed ordering where the model that is best at math is also the model that's best at jokes. Despite that complexity, much of the variation in performance is explained by just a single variable: model size. In general, models that are bigger will (a) be more performant / reliable, (b) cost more per token, and (c) have better recall of esoteric facts. As you note, our models are ordered:

 Luna < Terra < Sol < Astra

 [ ... ] These days, version number signifies a few things at once: the order of release, the relationship to other releases, and the magnitude of improvement. So something like 6.1 would indicate it was launched after 5.6, may share some similarities to other 6.1 models in terms of training data / personality (which is why it's not 5.7), and isn't a giant enough leap to merit the headlines and expectations that would come with a 7.
 
 — Ted Sanders , explaining OpenAI's model naming conventions

title: Why Agents Love Supabase
summary:
I first met Paul Copplestone and Ant Wilson in Singapore, shortly after they finished YC as the hottest startup of YC S20 . Six years later, we finally got them on the podcast! This is their first podcast together, after taking an open-source, fully remote company from zero to a $10 billion valuation. 

 The title is a question I wanted to understand for myself: why do agents love Supabase? There are plenty of managed databases. Postgres hosting is competitive. Being familiar to a model is useful distribution, but it doesn't explain all the work needed to turn a generated application into something that runs. But when I ran my frontier AEO tracker , it was an almost complete sweep of first choice for app backends (and in contention for managed db ) for every frontier model from Astra to Fable to Muse. 

 At Select, Supabase grouped its announcements into Build, Operate and Scale. 

 The things that stood out to me were surprisingly practical: start a local backend without Docker, keep the desired database schema in Git, and run compute beside the database. Each removes a piece of work that developers have been doing for years. Agents make that friction harder to ignore.

title: GitHub Octoverse 2026
summary:
GitHub Octoverse 2026 

I'm at GitHub Universe today (GitHub gave me a free ticket through their "GitHub Stars" program). EVP Jay Parikh just announced this year's Octoverse report, and highlighted these numbers in particular:

 This is a pretty stark representation of the impact of agentic engineering on GitHub. In 2026, merged pull requests tripled in less than a year to 220 million per month. Commits more than tripled to 7.38 billion per month, with most of that increase in the second half of this year. New repository rate doubled this year, to 30.3 million per month.

 The report includes new numbers by industry, and breaks out numbers for repositories that involve "interoperability or reverse engineering". The methodology section includes notes about how they did this: 

 Top countries by pushes to public repositories, adjusted by profile location . Pushes from each country were summed across the Octoverse year. title: The October inflection point for vibe game development
summary:
I've written before about how November 2025 was an inflection point for coding agents - the point where Opus 4.5 and GPT-5.1 crossed a tipping point that meant their respective coding agents became reliable daily drivers for software engineers. I think we've reached a new inflection point in October 2026, and this time it's for vibe coding computer games .

 Tree Appreciator 

 Emberwick 

 Battle Drones 

 Pumpkin Farmer, aka Quarter Sun Cove 

 Four times as insulting 

 What happens if someone actually puts the work in? 

 You should build a game! 

 Claude Opus 5.5 in particular exhibits meaningful improvements in several areas needed to build a compelling game:

 3D modeling

 Music generation (see Scrimshaw Jukebox )

 Game design (!)

 That last one is particularly important. Models have been able to create something that looks like a game for quite a while now, as seen in my previous experiments . The challenge has been getting to a game that's actually fun to play .

 Game design is a deep subject area. I won't pretend to be well versed in it - I know enough to have respect for it as a craft. Creating a novel, compelling gameplay loop which challenges players at the right level and provides a satisfying learning curve is a fine art. I didn't think the models could do it.

 Then I tried telling Claude Opus 5.5 to "Make it a LOT more fun"... and it did .

title: Artificial Analysis v5 and the benchmarker's dilemma
summary:
Housekeeping: I’m on the road so the voiceover will be late. Hill-climbing is easy, knowing what to hill-climb is hard. Making scores go up is expensive , but we have a much clearer playbook for it than we do for creating meaningful benchmarks at the true frontier of AI today.
 Independent evaluation of language models is under-appreciated in how hard of a task it is. These groups are not just taking current models and certifying their scores, which is a technically involved task. This is their job if AI progress is slow. When AI progress is as fast as it is, the technical details of the job are the routine work part of trying to put a single number on what makes for a good AI model today. The goal is to have a single number that is representative of current models, matching vibe checks, community sentiment, and scientific analysis, while being forward looking enough so that it’s not outdated in 3 months.
 Everyone building a benchmark faces a sort of paradox. You need your benchmark to reduce to one single number, so that it is easy to discuss, use in reports, and compare models, but every method of aggregating scores comes with meaningful trade-offs. The best scientists need to do this, everyone does. It’s a matter of creating aggregating metrics that you think are most fair, knowing there will always be imperfections.

title: Quoting Terk Terkowitz
summary:
If your work does not benefit from current AI tooling, that is a finding, not a failing. Document why, share it with your community of peers, bring it to your manager, and work to find solutions. An engineer who can explain where AI does not yet help their work is demonstrating the judgement we are asking for.
 
 — Terk Terkowitz , An update from Amazon engineering leadership on the role of the developer in the age of AI

title: [AINews] Anthropic ends Coding Interviews: "Hunger beats tenure"
summary:
Several midsize headlines today; on top of some impressive Math verification , Google Genie and Artificial Analysis and FrontierCode all shipped major version bumps of their top offerings, all of which have been AINews title stories in the past, but are mostly annual incremental improvements. 

 Past guest Felix Reiseberg gets the headline today for coming out and charting the path forward for junior engineers : “ Hunger beats tenure” 

 This month, I laid the traditional coding interview to rest. As a hiring manager at Anthropic, I stopped asking candidates to do them… 
 …There’s no more point in giving you a little React challenge than there is in quizzing people about assembly; Claude is now better at both. Our most impactful builders are successful regardless of how good they are at these tests.

 Enough said. 

 His advice for juniors 
 Pick business impact over backlog : In pre-AI-coding 2011, Patrick McKenzie wrote “engineers are hired to create business value, not to program things.” 

 Pick a radical idea : Come up with a few ideas that would, if successful, dramatically improve the chances that your organization achieves those goals. Be ambitious! 

 Build it over a weekend : I have seen small groups and solo engineers fly past the usual process of writing product requirements documents (PRDs), getting buy-in, and lobbying for time with designers or product managers by building a working prototype.
